# PR guidelines

This is the repository source for the DevOps PR process. Code standards live in [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md); agent instructions live in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Production changes, releases, and work intake remain in DevOps.

## Scope and structure

- Use one PR per Linear ticket. You may batch very minor, unrelated changes of a few lines when they are low risk.
- Scope the ticket to one specific problem. If additional problems need attention, pause that additional work and check with the team or lead before implementing it.
- Use separate PRs for unrelated refactors, feature additions, dependency updates, and lint or style fixes. Keep scope to a single package or app when possible.
- For features spanning packages, make foundational changes such as types and shared utilities first, then use separate PRs for usage and integration.

## Size and review guidance

About 200 added plus removed lines is a useful target. Up to 400 lines is acceptable when the change is scoped and self-contained. Ideally, touch fewer than five files; repetitive mechanical changes can justify more. These are review guidelines, not automatic rejection thresholds.

Test changes do not count toward the 400-line threshold.

Above 400 changed lines, explain why the PR cannot reasonably be split. Include the main review entry points and intended testing path in Reviewer brief. Keep this concise rather than adding a file-by-file summary.

## Branches and PR metadata

- Use Linear's generated branch name through Copy Branch Name.
- For Linear-backed work, use `ENG-#### Exact Linear ticket title` as the PR title. This is the repository convention in place of the alternative title formats previously listed in DevOps.
- Start with [.github/pull_request_template.md](.github/pull_request_template.md). Treat the ticket as the source of truth rather than restating it. Follow the PR body guidance in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#pull-request-bodies).

## Before requesting review

- Run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, then `pnpm ci:validate` from the repository root before opening a PR or declaring it ready. Resolve failures before requesting review. A draft must disclose unresolved validation blockers.
- Check applicable build and lint commands. Manually exercise changed behavior end-to-end, including relevant edge cases and alternative flows. Verification is optional; use it when checks and results help the reviewer.
- Read the complete final diff and review it against [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md), including added and modified comments. Use inline PR comments for review-specific explanations and durable code comments for constraints future changes must preserve.
- Run `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff. Paste its Scope check section into the PR body. If `Done When` is missing, leave the checkbox unchecked and state that explicitly.
- Run `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata. Check the Standards check box when it has run. Make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them.
- Complete the Local delegated full review required by the template, using `$dg-delegated-full-review` when no other full-review workflow is available.
- Include a Loom video for every PR, including backend, refactor, and infrastructure changes. Keep it under 2–3 minutes, show before/after for bug fixes, and narrate key decisions. Put the link in Loom video.
- Assign a reviewer when ready. Do not mark a draft ready while required evidence or reviews remain incomplete.

## After merge

Delete the PR branch after a successful merge. Creating a draft does not authorize merging or deleting branches.

It was a valid catch, and the stale side was the PR description, not `AGENTS.md`. I also found a second stale claim it missed: the docs still said we don't apply the severity downgrade, which stopped being true when I adopted `toWarns`.

## Verifying Done When

**"Errors match the community plugin scanner"**

| Method | Strength | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Review branch** on the directory entry | Ground truth | Blocked. Your scan fails at dependency install, so it won't return a comparable list |
| Replay v1.7.0: check out the tag, run `lint:scanner`, diff against the panel | Real oracle | Partly done. Both panel errors reproduce at exact file:line on current main. Running it against the actual v1.7.0 tree would be cleaner |
| Run `obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows@v1` with `scanner-lint: true` on a throwaway branch, diff its findings against ours | Strong proxy, Obsidian's own mirror | Not done. Also answers whether the Action works in this monorepo |
| Test asserting our resolved severities equal the published config's | Catches upstream drift | Not done |

The honest limit: the first row is the only thing that proves equality. Everything else proves we match Obsidian's *published description* of the scanner, which upstream issues [#178](https://github.com/obsidianmd/eslint-plugin/issues/178) and [#182](https://github.com/obsidianmd/eslint-plugin/issues/182) say diverges from the real bot.

**"Same error shows in CI and in the IDE"**

- **IDE**: you confirmed the red squiggles visually. That's real but not durable.

## Two things I'd add

1. **A plant-and-push test for CI.** One commit with `el.style.color = "red"`, confirm the check fails, revert. Cheap and decisive.
2. **An invariant test** asserting every rule in `errorRules` resolves in *both* `eslint.config.scanner.mjs` and `eslint.config.mjs`. Today the two surfaces are wired by hand, so someone can add a rule to one and not the other and nobody finds out until a release fails. This is the strongest available encoding of Done When, and it's small enough for this PR.

Want me to do either? I'd do both, in that order.

content.text:
Removed. All checks green on `a4227f55`, `MERGEABLE`.

## Where it came from

Me. It's not on main, and it wasn't needed.

I added it to `packages/eslint-config` so the IDE config could register the `eslint-comments` plugin for the four `eslint-comments/*` rules in `editorRules`. The scanner config never needed it: `obsidianmd.configs.recommended` already bundles and registers that plugin, so `...toWarns(recommended)` brings it along.

## Dropping it was also more correct

`recommended` exposes the plugin instance directly:

```
plugins exposed by recommended: obsidianmd, @typescript-eslint, no-unsanitized,
  import, @microsoft/sdl, depend, noUnsanitizedPlugin, eslint-comments, json
```

So `errorPlugins` now takes `eslint-comments` from there instead of a separate dependency. That removes a version-skew risk: our `^4.7.2` could have resolved to a different version than the one obsidianmd bundles, which is exactly the class of divergence we just spent effort eliminating by pinning the plugin.

The one thing a harvest costs is a dependency on upstream's internal shape, so I added a guard that throws if `eslint-comments` ever disappears from `recommended`. Without it, `plugins: { "eslint-comments": undefined }` would silently drop 42 findings from the editor and nobody would notice.

## Verified identical

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `lint:scanner` | 67 errors / 122 warnings | 67 / 122 |
| `pnpm lint` | 144 findings, 0 errors | 144, 0 |
| Blocking rules visible in IDE | 58 | 58 |
| `eslint-comments` findings in IDE | — | 42 |
| `check-types` | pass | pass |

The PR is now 8 files, 267 insertions, 2 deletions, with no source changes and one fewer dependency than before.

Still outstanding from the adherence check: Loom video, `$scope-check`, and the delegated full review. And my two verification offers stand: a plant-and-push test to prove the CI check actually goes red, and an invariant test that `errorRules` resolves in both configs.

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

The delegated review landed and it was worth running. CI green on `8b23b4b4`, `MERGEABLE`.

## It caught a bug I shipped

**`pnpm lint` was broken in `apps/obsidian`, exit 1.** Renaming the test to `.mts` made it match the typed block in `eslint.config.mjs` (`**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,cts}`) while `tsconfig.json` only included `**/*.ts`, so the parser couldn't find it in the project. `only-warn` doesn't downgrade parse errors.

My verification had a real gap: I ran `pnpm lint` *before* the rename, then only `tsc` and `vitest` after. `ci:validate` didn't catch it (it runs `check-types` and `test:unit`, not lint), and `lint-changed-files` skips `.mts`. Fixed by adding `**/*.mts` to the tsconfig include, which also means the test is now actually type-checked.

## And it corrected a claim I'd repeated

**The `extends` recursion is not load-bearing.** All 17 blocks of `recommended@0.4.1` are flat, zero use `extends`. I verified it. I told you that recursion was "the piece I was missing" and put it in the commit message and PR body. It was wrong. What actually made the Action's version work was something else in how I was assembling the config; I don't have a verified causal explanation, so I've stopped asserting one. The recursion stays as forward-compatibility with an honest comment.

## Other findings fixed

| Finding | Fix |
|---|---|
| `postcss.config.js` produced a permanent parse error | added to `allowDefaultProject` |
| VS Code escalation missed `eslint-comments/*` | added; that's 37 of the blocking findings that were still rendering yellow |
| Third test was tautological (`editorRules` is derived from `errorRules`) | replaced with a check that nothing is escalated in the config without being declared; mutation-tested, it fails correctly |
| `AGENTS.md` said the scanner is "deliberately separate from `pnpm lint`" | no longer true once the rules went into the main config; rewritten, including that `lint-changed-files` now gates them too |
| `no-implied-eval` duplicated the type-aware rule | dropped from `editorRules` |
| Plugin pinned in `apps/obsidian` but never imported there | removed |
| 5-line comment header over the 1–2 line limit | trimmed |

`lint:scanner` is now 65 errors / 121 warnings, down from 67, with no parse errors.

## One finding I disagree with

The reviewer flagged 13 `Definition for rule ... was not found` errors as "not Obsidian scanner findings." I don't think that's right: the real scanner doesn't register `preferArrows` or `react-hooks` either, so it would report the same errors. They're faithful predictions, not noise. I've documented that rather than registering those plugins, which would make us *less* like the scanner. Worth a reviewer's second opinion.

## Remaining

- **Bots**: Graphite reviewed and resolved; Devin's only review predates ~18 pushes; Codex has never posted. All three would need to re-review `8b23b4b4` for the babysit bar.

content.text:
Reproduced exactly, and this is a gap I built in. Not a bug in the rules.

```
A. pnpm lint  (what the IDE reads)
   178:13  warning  obsidianmd/no-static-styles-assignment
   (line 179: nothing)

B. lint:scanner  (what CI runs)
   178:13  error    obsidianmd/no-static-styles-assignment
   179:13  warning  obsidianmd/rule-custom-message   [no-console]
```

## Why

`lint:scanner` runs the **whole** rule set. The editor config registers only `editorRules`, which is the **error-level subset**.

`no-console` arrives via `obsidianmd/rule-custom-message`, which the scanner treats as a **warning**, not an error. So it's not in `errorRules`, so it's never registered in the editor, so there's no squiggle at all. The `.style` rule is error-level, so it is registered, and you see it.

So today: **IDE shows a strict subset of CI.** Every warn-level scanner finding is invisible in the editor. That's 121 findings.

## Making them match

The fix is to register the full scanner rule set in `eslint.config.mjs` instead of just the error subset. `defineConfig` handles it now, so the JSON-parser crash that blocked this early on is no longer a problem.

**But it has a side effect worth deciding on, not assuming.** `lint-changed-files` runs the main config through reviewdog with `-fail-level=warning` on added lines. So the moment those rules enter the main config, **every scanner warning becomes blocking on new code**. Adding a `setTimeout` would fail CI on `prefer-window-timers`; a `createElement` on `prefer-create-el`.

That's stricter than the scope you set earlier, when you said warnings don't matter because only errors block a submission. It's defensible (it stops new violations entirely), but it's a real change in day-to-day friction, and it's the opposite of that earlier call.

content.text:
That setting lives in `.vscode/settings.json` and belongs to the **ESLint editor extension**, not to ESLint itself.

## What it does

It recolors diagnostics the editor has already received. When ESLint reports a finding whose rule matches the glob, the extension renders it at the severity you name here.

- `obsidianmd/*` → every obsidianmd finding drawn as an error (red)
- `eslint-comments/*` → the four `eslint-comments` rules drawn as an error

## Why it's here

`packages/eslint-config/base.js` loads `eslint-plugin-only-warn`, which patches ESLint on import and forces **every** rule to `warn`. I confirmed an explicit `"error"` severity in config doesn't override it. So without this setting, a genuine submission blocker renders as ordinary yellow style advice, indistinguishable from the other 140 warnings in the file. This makes the blockers visually distinct again.

## What it does **not** do

This is the part that explains your `console.log`:

- **It cannot enable a rule.** It only restyles findings that ESLint already produced. `obsidianmd/rule-custom-message` isn't registered in `eslint.config.mjs`, so ESLint never reports it, so there is no diagnostic to recolor. No glob fixes that.
- **It has no effect outside your editor.** CI, `pnpm lint`'s exit code, and `lint:scanner` are all untouched. Someone editing in vim sees nothing from this line.
- **It's per-workspace**, so it only applies when the folder containing this `.vscode/settings.json` is your workspace root.

So the setting is doing its job on line 178 and is simply not involved on line 179.

## One flaw worth knowing

`obsidianmd/*` is a blunt glob. It paints *every* obsidianmd rule red. That's harmless today because only error-level ones are registered in the editor. But if we ever register the full scanner rule set, this would paint warn-level rules like `prefer-window-timers` red too, which would be wrong and would reintroduce exactly the confusion it was meant to remove. If we go that way, these globs need to become an explicit rule list.

content.text:
**No. It doesn't block CI, and I told you otherwise earlier.** That was true of an earlier design and I didn't flag when it stopped being true.

## Current behavior

| Job | fail level | Reports `console.log`? | Blocks? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `obsidian-scanner-lint` | `error` | yes, as a **warning** | **no** |
| `lint-changed-files` | `warning` | no, rule isn't registered in the main config | **no** |

So it blocks neither job, and it wouldn't block an Obsidian submission either: warnings don't block.

## What changed, and when

The earlier gate derived its rules by taking everything `recommended` marks as **error**, and `obsidianmd/rule-custom-message` (which is what reports `no-console`) **is** error-level there. Under that design your `console.log` genuinely would have failed CI, which is what I said at the time.

When I reworked the config to mirror the real scanner, I adopted the Action's severity model: downgrade everything, then re-escalate a specific list. `rule-custom-message` is **not** on that list, so it became a warning. That's the correct mirror of the real scanner, but it quietly removed `console.log` from the blocking set and I didn't surface the regression. That's the second time in this ticket a rework changed what blocks without me saying so.

## The part that's a separate problem

`apps/obsidian/AGENTS.md` says to minimize `console.log` and use `new Notice()` for user-facing errors. **Nothing enforces that today** — not the scanner config, not `pnpm lint`, not CI. It's prose only.

That's a house rule, not a scanner-fidelity question, and the two pull in opposite directions: matching the scanner means `no-console` is a warning; your team rule wants it blocking.

The narrow fix is one line in `apps/obsidian/eslint.config.mjs`:

```js
"no-console": ["error", { allow: ["warn", "error", "debug"] }]
```

That puts it in the main config, so it shows in the editor and `lint-changed-files` fails added lines carrying it, while `lint:scanner` keeps reporting it as the warning the real scanner reports. House rule and scanner mirror stay separate and both stay honest.

Direct answer: **our copy.** That step never contacts Obsidian. It runs ESLint with `eslint.config.scanner.mjs`, which re-exports `packages/eslint-config/obsidian-scanner.js` — a hand-port of two upstream sources.

## Three tiers of fidelity

| | What it is | Can drift? |
|---|---|---|
| `obsidian-scanner-lint` (our CI) | Our port of the published config plus the action's severity map | **Yes, silently.** Upstream changes and we don't notice |
| `obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows@v1` | Obsidian's own mirror. Generates the scanner config itself, pins its toolchain | Less. They maintain it. But its README only claims it "matches expectations", not that it's the production bot's code path |
| **Review branch** on community.obsidian.md | The actual scanner in Obsidian's sandbox | No. This is ground truth |

## Can we run the real workflow? Not against `apps/obsidian`

I checked `action.yml`. It declares seven inputs — `type`, `mode`, `build`, `lint`, `scanner-lint`, `strict`, `node-version` — and **no working-directory, path, or monorepo input**. It's a Node action (`using: node24`), so GitHub's `working-directory` doesn't apply to it either, and it auto-detects by looking for `manifest.json` at the repo root.

Ours is at `apps/obsidian/manifest.json`, so the action finds nothing. The only way to feed it would be a step that copies `apps/obsidian` to the workspace root first — at which point `@repo/database` and `@repo/utils` stop resolving, which is the same pnpm-workspace failure that made your v1.7.0 scan incomplete. So it would reproduce the bug rather than route around it.

**Review branch is the only way to run the real thing**, and it's free: it scans any branch, tag, or SHA without cutting a release.

## What would actually reduce our drift risk

A scheduled CI job that fetches upstream's `docs/configuration.md` and `obsidian-workflows/src/lint.ts`, hashes the relevant sections, and fails when they change. It wouldn't tell us *what* diverged, but it would stop us finding out at release time. That's a real guard and it's small.

Worth knowing we already have a live example of the risk: the action pins `eslint-plugin-obsidianmd@0.4.1` and upstream is on `0.4.2`. We pinned to match the action, but if Obsidian bumps the scanner and not the action, we follow the wrong one.

Traced it. The chain is three files.

## Where it's declared and read

**`action.yml`** declares the input:
> *"Use community scanner lint rulesets (stylelint + eslint-plugin-obsidianmd) instead of project config. Always forced to true in release mode."* — default `'false'`

**`src/index.ts`** is only `import { run } from './main.js'; run()`.

**`src/main.ts`** reads it and passes it through:
```ts
scannerLint: core.getInput('scanner-lint') === 'true',
...
await runLint(workspacePath, projectType, inputs.scannerLint, inputs.mode)
```

## What it actually does — `src/lint.ts`

```ts
export async function runLint(
  workspacePath: string,
  projectType: ProjectType,
  useScannerLint: boolean,
  mode: string
): Promise<Finding[]>
```

**`false` (default):** runs *your* lint. It looks for a `lint` script in `package.json` and runs `npm run lint`. Nothing Obsidian-specific happens.

**`true` (or `mode: release`, which forces it):**

1. Installs a **pinned toolchain into a scratch dir**, not your `node_modules` — `eslint@9.37.0`, `eslint-plugin-obsidianmd@0.4.1`, `typescript-eslint@8.61.1`, plus `stylelint@17.6.0` for CSS.
2. **Generates** `eslint.config.scanner.mjs` in that scratch dir, building the config string in code. This is the file our `obsidian-scanner.js` is ported from.
3. Runs `npx --prefix <scannerDir> eslint --config <configPath> --format json .` against your workspace.
4. Runs stylelint separately with the scanner's CSS ruleset, which we do **not** mirror at all.

So `scanner-lint: true` replaces your project's lint config with a freshly generated copy of the scanner's. It still isn't the production bot — same "mirror, not the thing" caveat as ours — but it's generated by Obsidian's code rather than hand-copied by me.

## The bit worth noting

`strict` (default `false`) downgrades failed **policy** findings from error to warning via `applyEnforcement`, and the action fails only on `status === 'failed' && severity === 'error'`. So even with `scanner-lint: true`, the default posture is laxer than a real submission review.

## Two gaps this exposes in ours

1. **We mirror only the ESLint half.** The action also runs stylelint with the scanner's ruleset against `styles.css`. We have a `styles.css` and we lint none of it. That's a whole category of findings we're blind to, and it's not in the PR.
2. **We pin to the action's versions, and the action can lag the real scanner.** It pins `0.4.1` while upstream is `0.4.2`.

A caveat on all of this: WebFetch summarizes through a model, so I'd treat the quotes as close paraphrase rather than guaranteed-verbatim. The clone that would have let me verify exactly was denied. If you want certainty on any specific line, approving a shallow clone would settle it.

Cloned [`obsidian-workflows` v1.2.3](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts) (`8167cae`) and diffed it against ours line by line.

## Provenance

`eslint.config.scanner.mjs` is **generated at runtime** by [`buildScannerEslintConfig()`](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L544) as a template string, written into a scratch dir, then run with `npx --prefix <scannerDir> eslint --config <path> --format json .`. Our `obsidian-scanner.js` is a hand-port of the string that function emits. There is no package to import; copying is the only option, which is why drift is the standing risk.

## 1-1 mapping

| Element | Action ([lint.ts](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts)) | Ours (`obsidian-scanner.js`) | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `toWarns` | [L578](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L578) | L8 | ✅ identical |
| `...toWarns(recommended)` | [L615](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L615) | L100 | ✅ |
| 6 security errors | [L627-633](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L627) | `errorRules` L30 | ✅ |
| 10 re-escalations | [L674-683](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L674) | `errorRules` L30 | ✅ |
| `no-unsafe-*` → off then warn | [L635-639, L666-670](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L635) | L112-116 | ✅ |
| `no-undef`, `restrict-template-expressions`, `no-base-to-string`, `import/no-unresolved` off | [L634-642](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L634) | L110-119 | ✅ |
| `validate-manifest` / `validate-license` off | [L644-645](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L644) | L121-122 | ✅ |
| `globalIgnores(IGNORES)` (30 entries) | [L549](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L549), sourced from `SCANNER_STYLELINT_CONFIG.ignoreFiles` [L13](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L13) | L130 | ✅ |
| **`no-restricted-disable` options** | not re-asserted, so `recommended`'s **12-entry** list survives | L49: hardcoded to **2 entries** | ❌ **we under-report** |
| **`commands/no-command-in-command-id`, `no-plugin-id-in-command-id`** | off at [L647-648](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L647), then **`warn`** at [L671-672](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L671) | off only | ❌ we drop 2 warnings |

The worst one is `no-restricted-disable`. `recommended` bans disabling 12 rules; I hardcoded 2. So a `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any` passes here and fails the real scan.

## The CSS scanner

A completely separate pass, [`SCANNER_STYLELINT_CONFIG` L11](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/main/src/lint.ts#L11), run with `stylelint@17.6.0` + `stylelint-no-unsupported-browser-features@8.1.1` against your CSS, config written to `.stylelintrc.scanner.json`.

Notable rules: external URLs in CSS are an **error** (only `data:` allowed), plus `declaration-no-important`, `color-named`, `property-disallowed-list: ['all']`, `at-rule-no-unknown`, and `plugin/no-unsupported-browser-features` whose browser target is **computed from your `manifest.json` `minAppVersion`** via an Electron version map.

Two things matter: it sets **`ignoreDisables: true`**, so stylelint-disable comments don't work, and we have an `apps/obsidian/styles.css` that is **currently unlinted by anything**.

content.text:
**Nothing legal stops us, and the test settles whether it's worth it: it is.**

## Upstream verbatim vs our port

I extracted the config `obsidian-workflows` actually generates and ran it, unmodified, against our code:

| | errors | warnings |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream, verbatim | 67 | 111 |
| Our port (after today's fixes) | 67 | 111 |
| Findings only in one of them | **0** | **0** |

Identical finding-for-finding, by file, line, column, rule and severity. So copying loses nothing, and it removes my hand-transcription as a source of error.

## What's actually stopping a literal copy of `lint.ts`

- **License: not a blocker.** Upstream is MIT, we're Apache-2.0. MIT code can go into an Apache project as long as we keep the MIT copyright and permission notice. That's the "tribute" you mean, and it's required, not optional.
- **`lint.ts` is the wrong unit.** It's 856 lines of GitHub Action runtime. It imports `@actions/core`, `@actions/exec`, and three local modules (`deps.js`, `detect.js`, `types.js`). It installs a toolchain into a temp dir, writes temp files, shells out to `npx`, and parses JSON into `Finding[]`. The config isn't even exported; it's a template string inside a private function. Copying the file gets you an Action, not a config.

**The right unit is the template body**, the `hasTsconfig` branch of `buildScannerEslintConfig()`. That's ~120 lines and it's exactly what the test above ran.

## What a verbatim copy would look like

```
packages/eslint-config/obsidian-scanner.js
├─ MIT notice + upstream URL + pinned commit (8167cae, v1.2.3)
├─ [verbatim] IGNORES, toWarns, the config array
└─ [ours, clearly marked] errorRules / editorRules / errorPlugins
```

Updating becomes "paste the new template", and the drift check we discussed becomes a literal text diff against upstream.

Two caveats:

- **It must live in `packages/eslint-config`.** My first attempt failed only because `apps/obsidian` can't resolve the plugin; I'd removed that dep on the reviewer's advice.
- **`errorRules` would duplicate the escalation list inside the copied block.** The existing invariant test already catches those two lists drifting apart, so this stays guarded.

## Something I should own

Upstream emits a plain array, not `defineConfig`, and it works. Earlier I told you `defineConfig` was the load-bearing piece, and before that the `extends` recursion. Both explanations were wrong. Each time I had a config that worked and wrote a confident story about why. The verbatim run is better evidence than any of those stories. That's also the strongest argument for copying: we stop depending on my reading of their code.

Want me to replace the port with the verbatim copy? I'd also bring along the stylelint half the same way — that's the next part of your question.

(CI on the cleaned-up branch is still running in the background; I'll report when it lands.)

git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
ENG-1832 Add Obsidian eslint to the project

The Obsidian community directory scans every plugin release with
eslint-plugin-obsidianmd. Errors block submission; warnings do not. Run
the same rules locally and in CI.

Adds `lint:scanner`, which runs the scanner's ESLint config. That config
is vendored verbatim from obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows (MIT), as the
output of its buildScannerEslintConfig() at commit 8167cae, and excluded
from Prettier so it stays diffable against upstream. A hand-written port
drifted from upstream in six places; the vendored copy produces identical
findings to the corrected port and removes that class of error.

Our own additions live separately in obsidian-scanner.js: the rules that
block a submission, registered in the app's eslint.config.mjs so editors
surface them. A test keeps that list in step with the vendored config.

The plugin is pinned to 0.4.1, the version that action installs.
`lint:scanner` needs its own config and process because
@repo/eslint-config loads eslint-plugin-only-warn, which patches ESLint
globally on import and forces every rule to "warn".

CI runs it through reviewdog with filter-mode=added, so existing findings
are reported without blocking while newly added ones fail.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

Done. The vendored config is in, and here's how stylelint works and how to match it.

## Replaced with the verbatim copy

The config now lives in two files:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `packages/eslint-config/obsidian-scanner.upstream.js` | The exact output of upstream's `buildScannerEslintConfig()`, generated from [their source at `8167cae`](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L544-L697) rather than retyped. It carries the MIT notice, the source link and the commit. It's in `.prettierignore` so formatting never changes it. |
| `packages/eslint-config/obsidian-scanner.js` | Only our additions: `errorRules`, `editorRules` and `errorPlugins`. It imports the config from the vendored file. |

What I verified:

- **Byte-identical to upstream.** The vendored file's body matches what their generator outputs, and it was still byte-identical after the commit hook ran.
- **Same findings.** Running it against our code gives 67 errors and 111 warnings, with zero differences from the previous port in either direction.
- **The test catches upstream changes.** I simulated an upstream release that escalates a new rule. The test failed and named the rule, so re-vendoring can't silently get ahead of the editor.
- The editor still shows the same 58 findings, and types pass.
- I staged only the three files this change touches. Your two work-in-progress files are still uncommitted.

CI for `256ff3be` is running in the background. One side effect: GitHub will mark the inline comments on `obsidian-scanner.js` as outdated, because `toWarns` moved into the vendored file. I can refresh them once you're happy with this layout.

## What the CSS scanner does

All of this is from the same file at [`8167cae`](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts):

1. **Finds CSS files.** [`findCssFiles()` L328](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L328) walks the plugin root and collects every `.css` file. It skips only `node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `.git` and `.obsidian`. The config's `ignoreFiles` then filters further, using the same 36-entry list as ESLint.
2. **Builds the config.** [`buildStylelintConfig()` L164](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L164) deep-copies [`SCANNER_STYLELINT_CONFIG` L11](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L11). It then sets the browser target from your `manifest.json` `minAppVersion`, through the [`ELECTRON_VERSIONS` map at L127](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L127). Our `minAppVersion` is `1.7.0`, which maps to `electron >= 30`.
3. **Runs stylelint.** It uses `stylelint@17.6.0` and `stylelint-no-unsupported-browser-features@8.1.1`, both pinned at [L172](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L172), and sets **`ignoreDisables: true`**. That means `/* stylelint-disable */` comments are ignored: you can't suppress a finding, only fix it.

**Severity is what matters.** Only one thing is an error: a `url()` with any scheme other than `data:`, such as `http`, `https` or `file`. That comes from two rules. `function-url-scheme-disallowed-list` is explicitly set to error, and `function-url-scheme-allowed-list: ['data']` has no severity, so stylelint applies its default, which is error. Every other rule is explicitly a warning: `!important`, `:has()`, named colours, unknown at-rules, unsupported browser features, and the rest.

[`parseStylelintOutput()` L199](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L199) tags every CSS finding as `enforcement: 'policy'`. In the Action's default non-strict mode, policy errors are downgraded to warnings, so the **Action** never fails on CSS. Whether the real directory scan blocks on a CSS error isn't visible in this code.

## Where our CSS stands

The scanner would find two files: `apps/obsidian/styles.css` and `src/styles/style.css`.

- **Error-level:** none, as far as I can tell without running stylelint. Every `url()` in our CSS is a `data:image/svg+xml` cursor. Those SVGs contain `http://www.w3.org/...` inside the data payload, which shouldn't count as a URL scheme, but a real run is the only way to be sure.
- **Warning-level:** 10 uses of `!important` and 7 of `:has()`. If `style.css` uses Tailwind directives such as `@tailwind` or `@apply`, expect `at-rule-no-unknown` warnings too, because the ignore list only allows `layer`, `property` and `container`.

## How to match it

Use the same approach as ESLint: vendor it, don't port it.

1. **Vendor the builder, not its output.** The output depends on `minAppVersion`, which comes from `manifest.json`. Baking it in would go stale the next time that changes. Instead, copy `SCANNER_STYLELINT_CONFIG`, `ELECTRON_VERSIONS`, `getMinElectronVersion()` and `buildStylelintConfig()` verbatim, with only the TypeScript types removed, under the same MIT notice. Then call the builder with `minAppVersion` read from `manifest.json` when the config loads.
2. **Name the file `apps/obsidian/stylelint.config.mjs`.** That's a name both the stylelint CLI and the VS Code stylelint extension find automatically. Stylelint has no equivalent of `only-warn`, so **the editor and CI will show identical severities**. The mismatch we just spent a week on doesn't exist for CSS.
3. **Pin the dependencies.** Add `stylelint@17.6.0` and `stylelint-no-unsupported-browser-features@8.1.1` as two new dev dependencies.
4. **Add a `lint:scanner:css` script** that runs `stylelint "**/*.css"` from `apps/obsidian`. The `ignoreFiles` list plus stylelint's default `node_modules` exclusion cover what `findCssFiles()` skips, apart from `dist`, `build` and `.git`, which we'd add to `ignoreFiles` on our side.
5. **Add a CI step** to the `obsidian-scanner-lint` job. Run stylelint with `--formatter unix` and feed the output to reviewdog with an `-efm` pattern. That needs no extra formatter dependency.

## Two open questions to settle before building

- **Is the root `styles.css` generated?** The build concatenates `src/styles/` into it, so the scanner may be reading built Tailwind output rather than source. If so, its findings belong to Tailwind's output, and we may need to lint the source file instead, or both.
- **Does a CSS error block a submission?** The Action treats CSS findings as non-blocking policy. The real scan's behaviour isn't in this code. Running **Review branch** on the directory entry would answer it.

**No change to `ci.yaml` for the vendoring.** I checked each job instead of assuming:

| Job | Touches the change? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `obsidian-scanner-lint` | Runs `eslint.config.scanner.mjs`, which still imports `{ config }`, now re-exported from the vendored file | ✅ passed on `256ff3be`; same command |
| `lint-changed-files` | Only lints workspaces that have an `eslint.config.mjs`. `packages/eslint-config` has none, so the vendored file is skipped | ✅ passed |
| `format-changed-files` | Runs `prettier --check` on changed files, and the vendored file is now in `.prettierignore` | ✅ locally, run the way CI calls it; CI still running |
| `validate` | Runs types and tests, including the invariant test | ✅ passed |

**One coupling worth knowing.** The vendored config sets `tsconfigRootDir: cwd()`, so it depends on the process's working directory. The CI step already runs `pnpm --dir apps/obsidian exec eslint`, which is correct. But if someone later changes it to run from the repo root, TypeScript resolution breaks. That's upstream's design and it's fine as long as that `--dir` stays.

## Stylelint would change it

Matching the CSS scanner means a **new step** in the `obsidian-scanner-lint` job, roughly:

```yaml
- name: Lint CSS against the Obsidian community scanner rules
  run: |
    pnpm --dir apps/obsidian exec stylelint "**/*.css" --formatter unix > "$css_output" || true
    reviewdog -efm="%f:%l:%c: %m" -name="obsidian-scanner-css" \
      -reporter=github-pr-check -filter-mode=added -fail-level=error < "$css_output"
```

The detail that needs care is **severity**. Stylelint's `unix` formatter writes severity as text at the end of each line, and a plain `-efm` pattern won't parse it, so reviewdog would treat every finding the same. Warnings like `!important` would then fail the build, unlike the scanner, where only non-`data:` URLs are errors. The fix is a small transform from stylelint's JSON output to reviewdog's `rdjson` format, which carries severity. That's a few lines of `jq`, so it's easy to get right but not something to hand-wave.

That's part of why I'd keep stylelint as a follow-up. The decision on generated `styles.css` and the severity mapping both deserve their own review.

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## TypeScript Guidelines

- Prefer `type` over `interface`
- Use explicit return types for functions
- Avoid `any` types when possible
- Prefer arrow functions over regular function declarations
- Use named parameters (object destructuring) when a function has more than 2 parameters

## Code Organization

- Prefer small, focused functions over inline code
- Co-locate code with its primary usage. Export it only for a concrete reuse need.
- Move code to `/utils` when it is shared across multiple call sites. Consider a shared package only after the code has stabilized and proven broadly reusable.
- Ground code movement in a current use case. Moving code because it feels cleaner adds churn without a clear functional benefit.
- Extract complex logic into well-named functions
- Prefer early returns over nested conditionals for better readability
- Function names should describe their purpose clearly:
## Documentation

- Use sentence case by default in docs and UI copy. Capitalize official product/plugin names and exact UI labels, buttons, or page titles, but keep generic feature terms lowercase.

## Code hygiene

- Remove unused imports, temporary comments, and debug logging before requesting review. Preserve intentional operational logging.
- Handle errors gracefully and log enough context to diagnose failures without exposing credentials or sensitive data.

## Testing

- Write unit tests for new functionality
- Ensure tests are meaningful and maintainable
- Cover relevant edge cases, error paths, and alternative flows.
- Expose workspace unit tests through a `test:unit` script so the root validation command includes them.

Done. The test is gone, the code comment is fixed, and both changes are pushed as `c7c9d7aa`. CI is running in the background.

## What changed

- **Test removed.** I also put back the two settings that only existed for it: the `**/*.mts` entry in `apps/obsidian/tsconfig.json` and the `{ts,mts}` glob in `vitest.config.mts`. Both now match main. The other unit tests (3 files, 21 tests) still pass, as do `pnpm lint` and type checking. `lint:scanner` gives the same results as before: 67 errors and 111 warnings.
- **Comment fixed.** The history note ("narrowed from 12 rules to 2") is gone, leaving the rule that lasts: *"The scanner passes eslint-comments/\* through unchanged, so its options must come from upstream."* The comment on `errorRules` used to point at the test. It now says plainly that nothing checks the list against the vendored config, so the two must be updated together.

## Why `obsidian-scanner.js` still exists, and why it doesn't need to

It exists for one thing: `errorRules`, a hand-written list of the 20 rules that block a submission, which the editor config needs. The vendored file already contains that information; the list just repeats it. The test was the only thing catching the two drifting apart, and with it gone the list is unguarded.

I checked whether we can stop maintaining that list. If I read the vendored config and collect every rule it ends up setting to `error`, I get **the same 20 rules, identical to the hand-written list**.

So `obsidian-scanner.js` can go:
- `eslint.config.scanner.mjs` would import the vendored config directly.
- `apps/obsidian/eslint.config.mjs`, now the list's only consumer, would read the blocking rules and their plugins from the vendored config. That puts the code next to its only use, which the style guide prefers.
- The hand-written list disappears, so it can no longer drift. That fixes the gap the test used to cover, without needing a test.

One filter stays: the editor still has to skip the two `no-unsanitized` rules, because that plugin isn't installed in `apps/obsidian`.

## Housekeeping after this push

The PR body's checkboxes refer to `256ff3be`, and it still mentions the test. Two of the inline comments also describe the test. I've left them alone for now: if you want `obsidian-scanner.js` removed, I'll make that change first and then re-run the three checks and refresh the body and comments once, instead of twice.

## Plugin Store Guidelines

The Obsidian community directory scans every release with
`eslint-plugin-obsidianmd`. Errors block your submission; warnings do not. Run
the same rules before opening a PR:

```
pnpm --dir apps/obsidian lint:scanner
```

`lint:scanner` runs in its own process and applies the scanner's own severity
mapping: everything downgraded to a warning except the security rules, the
`eslint-comments` rules, and the subset obsidianmd re-escalates. It needs its
own process because the shared repo config loads `eslint-plugin-only-warn`,
which forces every rule to "warn".

`pnpm lint` also reports the blocking rules, so they appear in the editor, but
only ever as warnings. Use `lint:scanner` when you need the real severities.
Note that `lint-changed-files` fails on warnings for lines a PR adds, so these
rules gate new code through both jobs.

The authoritative check is the directory itself: use **Review branch** on the
entry's management page at community.obsidian.md to scan any branch without
cutting a release. Obsidian also publishes `obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows` as a
GitHub Action that mirrors the scanner.

CI runs `lint:scanner` through reviewdog, so a finding on a line your PR adds
fails the build; pre-existing ones are reported but tolerated.
